questions.title: unique_ptr vs. shared_ptr: Choosing Ownership Semantics
questions.prompt: A colleague defaults to std::shared_ptr for every heap-allocated object 'to be safe.' When is that the right call, and when is std::unique_ptr clearly the better choice? Use a MarketDataCache shared by several subsystems as your shared-ownership example.
questions.modelAnswer: std::unique_ptr should be the default, not shared_ptr. unique_ptr has zero runtime overhead versus a raw pointer -- it's purely a compile-time wrapper that calls delete in its destructor -- and it correctly expresses the common case: exactly one piece of code owns this object. shared_ptr is for the genuinely less common case where ownership must be shared among multiple independent owners with no single piece of code that can say 'I'm done with this first' -- a MarketDataCache referenced by a pricing subsystem, a risk subsystem, and a logging subsystem, none of which knows when the others are finished with it, is a legitimate example: the cache should live until the last subscriber drops its reference. That flexibility costs something real: a shared_ptr carries a control block with an atomic reference count, and every copy and destruction performs an atomic increment or decrement -- measurable overhead in a tight loop, and more memory per pointer than a unique_ptr. Defaulting to shared_ptr 'to be safe' usually just means nobody thought carefully about who owns what, and it hides a design question behind reference counting rather than answering it.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd push back gently: shared_ptr isn't a safety net, it's a specific tool for a specific ownership shape, and most code doesn't actually have that shape. If I can point to one piece of code that's clearly responsible for an object's lifetime, unique_ptr is strictly better -- same safety, zero reference-counting cost. I'd reserve shared_ptr for something like a market data cache that three unrelated subsystems all hold onto independently, where there genuinely isn't a single owner. Reaching for shared_ptr everywhere usually means the ownership question was never actually answered, just paved over.
commonMistakes: Defaulting to shared_ptr everywhere instead of unique_ptr, paying reference-counting overhead for no reason
Believing shared_ptr is 'thread-safe' in general, when only the reference count itself is atomic -- the pointed-to object still needs its own synchronization
Creating shared_ptr cycles (A holds a shared_ptr to B, B holds one back to A), causing a leak that shared_ptr alone can't detect
keyPoints: unique_ptr has zero overhead versus a raw pointer and should be the default
shared_ptr is for genuine multi-owner scenarios with no single clear owner
shared_ptr's reference count is atomic, costing real overhead on copy/destroy
Reference counting is not a substitute for a clear ownership design

Explains the real overhead cost of shared_ptr

questions.title: Move Constructor, std::move, and What Actually Happens at Runtime
questions.prompt: Explain the difference between a copy constructor and a move constructor, what std::move actually does at runtime, and why marking a move constructor noexcept matters.
questions.modelAnswer: A copy constructor duplicates another object's resources -- for a struct holding a std::vector, that means allocating a new buffer and copying every element. A move constructor instead transfers ownership of the other object's internal resources -- for the same vector member, PriceSeries(PriceSeries&& other) : prices(std::move(other.prices)) just chains down to vector's own move constructor, which swaps a few internal pointers (data, size, capacity), leaving `other` empty, with zero element copying. std::move itself does nothing at runtime -- it performs no computation and moves no bytes. It is purely a cast that converts an lvalue into an rvalue reference, which makes the move overload eligible to be selected by overload resolution instead of the copy overload. Marking a move constructor noexcept matters because several standard library optimizations specifically check for it: when std::vector reallocates during growth, it will move its elements into the new buffer instead of copying them only if the element type's move constructor is noexcept; if it isn't, vector falls back to copying for exception-safety reasons (so that a half-moved vector never ends up in a state where it has lost some elements but an exception unwound the operation).
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd draw the line like this: copy duplicates, move steals. std::move is just a label -- it tells the compiler 'you're allowed to treat this as disposable,' and the actual transfer happens inside whichever move constructor gets selected as a result, usually just a pointer swap. The noexcept detail trips people up because it feels like a minor annotation, but it directly changes vector's reallocation behavior -- an un-noexcept move constructor on your element type means vector quietly falls back to copying on every growth, silently eating the performance win you thought you had.
commonMistakes: Believing std::move performs the transfer itself, rather than just enabling overload resolution to pick the move constructor
Using a's contents after std::move(a) without reassigning or reconstructing it first
Forgetting to mark a hand-written move constructor noexcept, silently losing vector's move-on-reallocation optimization
keyPoints: Copy constructors duplicate resources; move constructors transfer ownership
std::move is a cast with no runtime effect of its own
After being moved from, an object is in a valid but unspecified state
noexcept on a move constructor enables std::vector to move instead of copy during reallocation

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes copy vs. move constructor behavior
Correctly explains std::move as a cast with no runtime action
Explains the noexcept/vector-reallocation interaction correctly

questions.title: std::vector vs. std::list for a Reused, Filtered Intermediate Result
questions.prompt: You have 200,000 intermediate order records that will be iterated over, in full, three separate times with different filters. A teammate suggests std::list because 'we might insert into the middle later.' Which container do you choose, and why does cache locality matter more here than the Big-O argument for insertion?
questions.modelAnswer: std::vector is the right choice here, and the Big-O argument for std::list's O(1) middle insertion is beside the point for a workload that's 95% iteration. std::vector stores its elements contiguously, so each 64-byte cache-line fetch during iteration pulls in several consecutive elements at once -- sequential scans run close to memory bandwidth. std::list is a doubly-linked list where each element is its own separately heap-allocated node, scattered across the heap in whatever order the allocator happened to place them; every `++it` is a pointer chase that's very likely a fresh cache miss, costing roughly 100ns instead of roughly 1-10ns for an L1/L2 hit. Over three full passes across 200,000 elements, that constant-factor cache penalty on every single element dwarfs the theoretical advantage of O(1) insertion -- an advantage that only matters if insertions into the middle are actually frequent and the container is large, not 'might happen later.' The professional default is: reach for std::vector, and only reconsider once you've measured a real, current reason insertion in the middle at scale is the actual bottleneck.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd tell them: let's not design around a 'might' -- right now the measured access pattern is three full scans, and for that, vector wins decisively regardless of what the complexity tables say about insertion. A list's O(1) insertion is real, but every single step of iterating it is a likely cache miss because the nodes are scattered across the heap; vector's contiguous layout means iteration is close to free by comparison. If and when we actually have a workload that's dominated by frequent middle-insertions at real scale, that's the point to revisit it -- and even then I'd want to measure before assuming list wins, because vector with an occasional shift-and-insert often still comes out ahead in practice.
commonMistakes: Choosing a container based on Big-O insertion cost without accounting for cache-locality constant factors
Designing for a hypothetical future access pattern instead of the actual, current one
Assuming std::list's O(1) insertion claim translates directly into real-world speed at any container size
keyPoints: std::vector's contiguous layout makes sequential iteration cache-friendly
std::list's scattered nodes make iteration cache-unfriendly despite O(1) insertion
A workload dominated by iteration should pick vector regardless of insertion complexity
Measure actual access patterns rather than designing for hypothetical future ones

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly recommends std::vector for this workload
Explains cache-line/contiguous-memory reasoning correctly
Correctly frames why Big-O alone is misleading here

questions.title: Implement a Thread-Safe Trade Counter With std::atomic
questions.prompt: Two threads record trades concurrently by incrementing a shared counter. Implement it so there's no data race, without using a mutex, and explain which memory ordering you chose and why.
questions.modelAnswer: Declare the counter as std::atomic<long> and increment it with fetch_add, which performs the read-add-write as a single indivisible step that no other thread can observe half-finished. For a plain counter where only the final total matters -- nobody needs to know when a particular increment happened relative to other memory -- std::memory_order_relaxed is the correct and fastest choice: it still guarantees atomicity of the increment itself, just without imposing any ordering constraint on surrounding memory operations, which a counter doesn't need. This is faster than a mutex-protected increment because there's no possibility of blocking; the operation either succeeds in one step or, for a compare-exchange-based structure, retries, but fetch_add itself is a single hardware instruction on most platforms and never blocks.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd reach for std::atomic<long> and fetch_add(1, std::memory_order_relaxed) without a second thought here. The reasoning on memory_order_relaxed specifically: relaxed only promises the increment itself can't be torn or lost -- it says nothing about how operations around it get reordered, and for a counter where the only thing that matters is the final total, that's exactly the guarantee I need and nothing more. If I were instead publishing some other piece of data alongside a flag -- 'this data is ready now' -- I'd reach for acquire/release instead, because then the ordering between the data write and the flag actually matters. Picking the weakest ordering that's still correct is the right habit, not reflexively defaulting to seq_cst everywhere.
commonMistakes: Using a mutex to protect a simple counter when fetch_add is both simpler and faster
Reaching for memory_order_seq_cst by default without considering whether relaxed is sufficient and correct
Still performing trade_count = trade_count + 1 on the atomic without realizing compound read-modify-write needs fetch_add, not separate load/store
keyPoints: std::atomic<T>::fetch_add performs an indivisible read-modify-write
memory_order_relaxed is sufficient when only the final value matters, not timing relative to other memory
Atomics avoid blocking entirely, unlike a mutex
Choosing the weakest correct memory ordering is the professional default, not always seq_cst

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly implements the counter with std::atomic and fetch_add
Chooses and justifies memory_order_relaxed correctly
Explains why this avoids blocking versus a mutex

questions.title: Bind a C++ Bond Pricer to Python With pybind11
questions.prompt: Write the pybind11 binding code that exposes a C++ Bond class (constructor taking face value, coupon rate, and years; a price(yield) method) to Python, with keyword-argument support, and show how it would be called from Python.
questions.modelAnswer: Binding a class in pybind11 uses py::class_<T>(m, "PythonName"), chaining .def(py::init<...>()) for the constructor with the C++ argument types listed as template parameters, and .def("method_name", &T::method) for each method. py::arg("name") attaches a keyword-argument name to each parameter, both for the constructor and for methods, so Python callers can use Bond(face_value=1000.0, coupon_rate=0.05, years=10) and bond.price(yield=0.04) exactly as if Bond had been written natively in Python. Once the module is compiled (a separate build step), the C++ class behaves like an ordinary Python object, with pybind11 handling all the argument type conversion (double, int) automatically -- no manual reference counting or marshaling code needed on either side.
questions.professionalAnswer: This is close to boilerplate once you've done it a few times: py::class_ for the type, .def(py::init<...>()) for the constructor with py::arg names so Python callers get keyword arguments, then one .def(...) line per method you want exposed. The part worth calling out in an interview is that pybind11 is handling the type conversion for you -- double and int cross the boundary with zero manual marshaling -- which is exactly the convenience that breaks down once you want to pass a NumPy array instead of a scalar, which is a fair follow-up question to expect.
commonMistakes: Forgetting py::arg(...) names, which breaks keyword-argument calls from Python
Omitting py::init<...>() and expecting pybind11 to guess the constructor signature
Assuming this same automatic-conversion approach will work unchanged once a NumPy array parameter is introduced
keyPoints: py::class_<T> binds a C++ class; .def(py::init<...>()) binds its constructor
py::arg("name") enables Python keyword arguments for both constructors and methods
pybind11 automatically converts scalar types (double, int) across the boundary
Compiled modules behave like ordinary Python imports once built

questions.title: Find and Fix the Dangling Reference
questions.prompt: Review this code. It compiles cleanly but has undefined behavior. Identify the bug and fix it.
questions.modelAnswer: The bug is that getBestBid() returns a reference (const double&) to a local variable, best, which is destroyed the moment the function returns -- the caller receives a reference to memory that's already gone, and reading through it is undefined behavior, exactly the same category of bug as returning a raw pointer to a local. It can appear to 'work' in testing because the stack memory often still holds the old bit pattern briefly, which is precisely what makes this bug dangerous rather than merely broken. The fix is to return by value: double getBestBid() const { ... return best; } -- modern C++'s move/copy elision makes this just as cheap as returning a reference would have been if it were actually safe, so there's no performance reason to prefer the broken version.
questions.professionalAnswer: This is the classic 'reference to a local' bug, just dressed up as a member function instead of a free function -- same root cause as returning a pointer to a stack variable, just easier to miss because a reference doesn't look like a pointer. The fix is simple: return by value. People sometimes resist that because 'returning by reference avoids a copy,' but for a double that's a non-argument, and even for a larger type, modern C++ makes return-by-value cheap via moves -- there's no real performance reason left to keep the dangerous version.
commonMistakes: Mistaking this for a pointer bug only, not recognizing that references have the exact same dangling-lifetime hazard
Assuming the code is correct because it compiles without warning and may even run without crashing
'Fixing' it by making best static, which hides the symptom but introduces a shared-state bug across calls instead
keyPoints: Returning a reference to a local variable is undefined behavior, identical in nature to returning a dangling pointer
Undefined behavior can appear to work by coincidence, which is exactly why it's dangerous
Returning by value is the correct fix and is cheap under modern move semantics
Making the local static is not a real fix -- it introduces shared mutable state

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the dangling-reference bug
Provides the correct fix (return by value)
Explains why this is undefined behavior rather than merely inefficient

questions.title: Diagnosing an Intermittent Data Race
questions.prompt: A pricing engine occasionally produces a slightly wrong number under load, but never in single-threaded testing, and the bug doesn't reproduce reliably. How would you confirm this is a data race, and what tool would you reach for before trying to reason about it by eye?
questions.modelAnswer: The symptom pattern -- wrong only under concurrent load, never single-threaded, and not reliably reproducible -- is the classic signature of a data race, because a race's outcome depends on the OS scheduler's exact, largely unpredictable interleaving of threads, not on the input data. Reasoning about this by eye across a real codebase is unreliable and slow; the right first move is to rebuild with ThreadSanitizer (-fsanitize=thread) and run the exact same concurrent workload that triggers the bug under that instrumented build. ThreadSanitizer tracks every memory access across threads and reports the precise pair of racing accesses -- which two threads, which memory location, which lines of code -- the moment they actually race during that run, rather than requiring the bug's symptom (the wrong price) to be the thing you chase. Once TSan points at the specific shared variable, the fix is standard: protect it with a mutex, make it a std::atomic if it's a simple value, or restructure so it's no longer shared mutable state. Testing alone can never prove the race is gone, since 'it passed this run' says nothing about the next one; TSan (or careful reasoning about every piece of shared state) is what gives real confidence.
questions.professionalAnswer: The moment I hear 'wrong only under load, never single-threaded, not reliably reproducible,' I stop trying to spot it by reading code and go straight to ThreadSanitizer. Rebuild with -fsanitize=thread, run the same concurrent load that triggers it, and let TSan point at the exact racing memory access -- it'll name the two threads and the exact lines. Trying to find a race by code review alone on anything non-trivial is a losing game; the whole point of a data race is that its effect depends on scheduling you can't fully control or predict by inspection.
commonMistakes: Trying to spot the race by code review alone instead of reaching for ThreadSanitizer
Concluding the bug is fixed because a single test run passed after a change, when the race is schedule-dependent
Assuming any random-looking wrong number under load must be a floating-point issue rather than considering a race first
keyPoints: Intermittent, load-dependent wrongness that never reproduces single-threaded is a classic data-race signature
ThreadSanitizer (-fsanitize=thread) directly reports the racing memory access and threads involved
A data race's outcome depends on unpredictable OS scheduling, not deterministic inputs
Passing a test run is not proof a race is fixed

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the symptom pattern as a likely data race
Names and correctly describes using ThreadSanitizer
Explains why testing alone can't prove correctness
Clarity

questions.title: Diagnosing a Slow Hot Loop Caused by Allocation
questions.prompt: Profiling shows a pricing loop spends most of its time inside std::vector's internal allocator, not inside the actual math. The loop builds a vector of results by push_back-ing one at a time, millions of times per second. What's going on, and how do you fix it?
questions.modelAnswer: Without a prior call to reserve(), std::vector grows by reallocating to a larger buffer and copying (or moving) every existing element into it each time push_back exceeds current capacity -- typically doubling capacity each time. For a loop called millions of times per second, that pattern means repeated heap allocation requests and repeated bulk moves of already-placed elements, which shows up in a profiler as time spent inside the allocator rather than inside the actual pricing math, exactly as described. The fix is to call .reserve(n) once, up front, with a known or reasonably estimated final size, turning the many reallocate-and-copy cycles into a single allocation; push_back calls after that just write into already-allocated capacity with no further allocator involvement. If the vector is rebuilt on every call of a hot function, an additional fix is to allocate it once outside the loop and .clear() and reuse the same buffer on each call -- clear() keeps the already-allocated capacity, so there's no repeated allocate/free cycle across calls either.
questions.professionalAnswer: The profiler pointing at the allocator rather than the math is the tell -- that's not a 'the algorithm is slow' problem, it's a 'we're asking the heap for memory way more than we need to' problem. First thing I'd check is whether reserve() was ever called; if the final size is knowable or estimable, one reserve() turns a dozen reallocate-and-copy cycles into exactly one allocation. If this vector gets rebuilt fresh on every call of a hot function, I'd go further and hoist it outside the loop entirely, reusing the same buffer with clear() between calls -- that avoids paying for allocation and deallocation on every single invocation, not just within one pass.
commonMistakes: Blaming the math/algorithm when the profiler is actually pointing at allocator time
Calling reserve() with a guess that's too small, which still triggers reallocations past that point
Reallocating a fresh vector on every function call instead of reusing one outside the hot loop
keyPoints: push_back without reserve() triggers repeated reallocate-and-copy cycles as capacity is exceeded
reserve(n) turns that into a single up-front allocation when n is known or estimable
clear() preserves capacity, letting a buffer be reused across repeated calls without reallocating
Profiler time inside the allocator, not the math, is the signal to look at allocation pattern first

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses repeated reallocation from push_back without reserve
Prescribes reserve() as the primary fix
Mentions reusing a buffer across calls via clear() as an additional fix

questions.title: REST vs. FIX vs. Native Broker APIs: Choosing a Connectivity Protocol
questions.prompt: A trading system needs to connect to a new venue. The venue offers a REST API, a FIX endpoint, and its own native SDK. What tradeoffs would you weigh in choosing among them, and does the strategy code need to know which one was chosen?
questions.modelAnswer: REST is the simplest to integrate -- plain HTTP requests with JSON responses -- but typically has higher latency and no persistent push connection, so fills usually require a separate WebSocket or polling mechanism alongside it. FIX is the institutional standard: a persistent, stateful session with lower latency and well-defined semantics for orders and execution reports, but materially more complex to implement correctly, with session management, sequence numbers, and message recovery after a disconnect all needing careful handling. The venue's native SDK is often the fastest path to get something working for that specific venue, at the cost of locking the integration into that venue's own abstractions, which becomes a real cost the moment a second venue needs to be added. The choice depends on latency requirements and integration timeline: a latency-sensitive HFT venue connection probably justifies FIX's complexity; a lower-frequency or exploratory integration might reasonably start with REST or the native SDK. Critically, none of this should leak into the strategy code -- an OMS abstraction layer sits between the strategy and whichever protocol was chosen, so the strategy calls a stable submit/cancel interface regardless of what's underneath, and switching protocols later (or adding a second venue with a different protocol) touches only the OMS implementation, not every strategy.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd weigh it mostly on latency requirement versus integration effort: REST is the fastest to get working and fine if we're not latency-sensitive on this venue; FIX is more work up front -- session state, sequence numbers, reconnect logic -- but it's the right call if this venue actually needs to be fast. The native SDK is tempting because it's often the quickest path, but I'd be wary of letting that lock us into venue-specific abstractions throughout the codebase. Either way, the strategy code itself shouldn't know or care which protocol we picked -- that decision lives entirely inside the OMS layer, so if we're wrong today, fixing it later doesn't mean touching every strategy that trades on this venue.
commonMistakes: Letting strategy code call a venue's native SDK or REST client directly, bypassing the OMS abstraction
Choosing FIX reflexively as 'the professional choice' without weighing actual latency requirements against its real integration cost
Underestimating FIX session management (sequence numbers, reconnect/recovery) as 'just another API to call'
keyPoints: REST trades simplicity for higher latency and lacks a persistent push connection on its own
FIX offers lower latency and institutional standardization at real integration complexity cost
A native SDK is quick to integrate but creates venue lock-in
The OMS abstraction layer should isolate the strategy code from whichever protocol is chosen

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly characterizes REST/FIX/native tradeoffs
Ties the choice to actual latency requirements, not reflexive preference
States that strategy code should remain protocol-agnostic via the OMS layer

questions.title: Choosing Between a Vectorized and Event-Driven Backtest Engine
questions.prompt: A researcher wants to add a trailing stop-loss to their strategy, which has so far been backtested with a fully vectorized pandas implementation. Explain why this specific feature is a problem for the vectorized approach, and what engine design actually handles it cleanly.
questions.modelAnswer: A vectorized backtest expresses the whole strategy as array operations computed over the full price history at once -- it implicitly assumes every bar's decision can be computed independently from simple array math (e.g. comparing a fast and slow moving average column-wise). A trailing stop-loss breaks that assumption because it's path-dependent: whether the stop fires on a given bar depends on the sequence of what happened since the position was entered -- specifically, the running maximum (or minimum) price reached since entry -- not on that bar's data in isolation. You can sometimes force path-dependent logic into vectorized form with clever tricks (a cumulative-max column, conditional resets), but past a certain complexity it becomes harder to trust the vectorized code than to simulate the path directly. An event-driven engine handles this cleanly because it iterates through time bar by bar, maintaining ordinary mutable state (the position's entry price, its running high-water mark) as plain variables that get updated each step -- the stop-loss check is just an ordinary if-statement against that running state, exactly the kind of thing a sequential loop expresses naturally and a whole-array operation does not.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd tell the researcher: a trailing stop is exactly the kind of rule that breaks the vectorized model's core assumption, because whether it fires today depends on the path the price took since you entered, not just today's row. You can sometimes hack a cumulative-max column into the vectorized version, but it gets fragile fast, and at that point you're fighting the tool. An event-driven backtest just tracks the position's high-water mark as a normal variable and checks it against the stop level bar by bar -- it's slower, but the logic is natural and obviously correct, which is exactly the tradeoff event-driven engines are for.
commonMistakes: Trying to force increasingly complex path-dependent logic into a vectorized backtest instead of switching engines
Not recognizing a trailing stop as path-dependent and assuming it's just another column-wise comparison
Assuming event-driven is strictly 'better' rather than understanding it as a deliberate speed/realism tradeoff
keyPoints: Vectorized backtests assume each bar's decision is independent, simple array math
A trailing stop-loss is path-dependent -- it needs a running high-water mark since entry
Event-driven engines maintain ordinary mutable state bar by bar, making path-dependent logic natural
Neither approach is universally better; they trade speed against realism/expressiveness

Explains why vectorization struggles with path-dependence

questions.title: Explaining a Latency/Correctness Tradeoff to a Non-Technical PM
questions.prompt: Your product manager asks why the new pricing path can't just use the fastest possible shortcut you mentioned in standup, and wants it live by Friday. The shortcut trades a small amount of numerical precision for a meaningful latency win. How do you explain the tradeoff and the risk, without the conversation turning technical?
questions.modelAnswer: The right approach is to translate the tradeoff into business terms the PM actually cares about, not into the technical mechanism. Concretely: state what's gained (a specific, meaningful latency number, and what that means competitively -- faster quotes, better fill rates), state what's risked in plain terms (prices could be off by a tiny, usually negligible amount, but in rare edge cases that small error could compound into a real, visible mispricing), and give a concrete recommendation with a reason, not just a worry: for example, ship it behind a flag on a low-risk subset of instruments first, measure the actual error distribution in production, then expand -- rather than a binary yes/no on a hard deadline. This keeps the PM in a position to make an informed business decision (how much risk is acceptable for how much speed) instead of either rubber-stamping something they don't understand or getting lost in floating-point details that aren't actually the decision they need to make.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't try to explain the floating-point mechanics -- that's not actually what they need to decide. I'd say something like: this gets us a real latency win, here's roughly how much, and here's the actual cost -- a small chance of a pricing error that's usually negligible but could occasionally matter. Then I'd give them an actual path forward instead of a flat no: let's ship it on a limited set of instruments first, watch the real error numbers in production, and expand once we've seen it behave. That turns 'can we ship by Friday' into a decision they can actually own, instead of me either blocking them outright or quietly shipping something risky because the deadline pressure won.
commonMistakes: Explaining the technical mechanism in detail instead of the business-relevant tradeoff
Giving a flat yes or no without offering a staged, risk-managed path forward
Letting deadline pressure silently ship a risk the PM never actually understood or agreed to
keyPoints: Translate technical risk into business terms: what's gained, what's risked, in plain language
Offer a concrete, staged path forward rather than a binary yes/no under deadline pressure
Keep the PM able to make an informed decision rather than overwhelming or under-informing them
Don't let schedule pressure cause a risk to ship without being explicitly understood and accepted

questions.title: Code Review Discipline Under Deadline Pressure
questions.prompt: You're reviewing a teammate's pull request that touches the order-submission path, and the release is due in two hours. The code looks mostly fine but you notice a missing null check and a questionable retry loop. How do you handle the review?
questions.modelAnswer: The order-submission path is exactly the kind of code where a shortcut under deadline pressure has outsized downside -- a missing null check or a bad retry loop there can mean a duplicated or lost order with real money attached, not a cosmetic bug. The right approach is to separate 'what must be fixed before merge' from 'what can be a fast follow,' rather than treating the deadline as a reason to wave everything through or, at the other extreme, blocking the release over something genuinely minor. A missing null check and a questionable retry loop on an order-submission path are both squarely in the 'must fix before merge' category, because they're correctness issues on money-moving code, not style preferences. I'd flag both specifically and concretely -- not just 'this looks risky' but exactly which input could be null and exactly which retry scenario could duplicate an order -- and offer to pair on the fix immediately rather than just blocking and walking away, since the goal is getting a safe version out in two hours, not winning a review.
questions.professionalAnswer: On the order path specifically, I don't compromise on correctness issues just because the clock is ticking -- that's exactly the code where a shortcut turns into a real incident, not an inconvenience. I'd call out the null check and the retry loop specifically, with the exact scenario each one breaks, and immediately offer to pair on the fix rather than just leaving a comment and disappearing -- the goal in the next two hours is a safe release, not a long review thread. If there were lower-stakes issues in the same PR -- a naming nit, a missing comment -- I'd happily let those go as a fast follow so we're not blocking a real deadline over something that genuinely doesn't matter tonight.
commonMistakes: Approving a PR with known correctness issues on money-moving code because of deadline pressure
Blocking a release over genuinely minor style issues, treating every comment as equally urgent
Leaving vague feedback ('this seems risky') instead of naming the exact failure scenario
keyPoints: Correctness issues on order-submission/money-moving code are not negotiable under deadline pressure
Separate must-fix-before-merge issues from legitimate fast-follow items
Give specific, concrete feedback naming the exact failure scenario, not vague concern
Offer to actively help fix the issue rather than only flagging and blocking

questions.title: Handling a Disagreement With a Trader About a Risky Deploy
questions.prompt: A trader wants a change to the execution logic pushed live immediately before market open because it should improve fill rates, but you haven't finished testing its interaction with the kill-switch logic. How do you handle the disagreement?
questions.modelAnswer: The core of this disagreement is a real tradeoff -- a plausible fill-rate improvement versus an unverified interaction with the system's hard risk control -- and the right response is to make that tradeoff explicit rather than simply saying no or simply complying. I'd state clearly, in concrete terms: what's untested specifically (the interaction between the new execution logic and the kill-switch), what could go wrong if it's wrong (a kill-switch that doesn't trigger correctly, or triggers incorrectly, under the new logic), and what the actual cost of waiting is (missing today's session, not missing the opportunity permanently). I'd offer a concrete alternative rather than a flat refusal -- for example, deploy it on a small subset of symbols or size first, with the existing kill-switch logic double-checked against that specific change in a lower-stakes way, or delay by one session to finish the specific test that matters, rather than the whole test suite. The kill-switch is exactly the kind of control that exists precisely for the moment someone is confident a change is fine -- deploying an unverified interaction with it under time pressure is the scenario it's designed to protect against, which is the concrete reason to hold the line rather than defer to urgency alone.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't just say 'no, not tested' and leave it there, because that doesn't actually resolve anything for the trader who has a real, time-sensitive reason to want this live. I'd be specific: here's exactly what's unverified -- how this interacts with the kill-switch -- and here's what breaks if that interaction is wrong, which is the one safety net we have for exactly this kind of situation. Then I'd offer something real: can we ship it on a small slice today while I finish verifying the kill-switch interaction, or is one more session really that costly compared to shipping an unverified change into our hard risk control? Usually once it's framed as 'the kill-switch is specifically the thing protecting us from being wrong about this,' the urgency argument loses most of its force.

questions.title: Why cv.wait Needs a Predicate, Not Just a Notification
questions.prompt: A teammate writes cv.wait(lk); with no predicate argument, relying purely on cv.notify_one() to wake the consumer at the right time. What two specific hazards does this expose the code to, and why does passing a predicate to wait fix both?
questions.modelAnswer: The bare cv.wait(lk) form is exposed to two distinct hazards. First, a spurious wakeup: the OS is explicitly allowed to wake a waiting thread without any notify_* call ever happening, so the thread can resume even though nothing it's waiting for actually changed. Second, a missed notification: if notify_one() is called before the consumer thread has actually started waiting (a real timing possibility, since producer and consumer run concurrently), that notification is simply lost -- there's no queued-up 'wake up' signal sitting around for the consumer to receive once it does call wait. Passing a predicate -- cv.wait(lk, [] { return !queue.empty(); }) -- fixes both at once: internally, this is shorthand for 'unlock, sleep, wake up (for any reason, spurious or real), re-lock, and then actually check the predicate; if it's false, go back to sleep.' A spurious wakeup just gets re-checked and, finding the predicate false, goes right back to sleep with no observable effect. A missed notification is also harmless, because the predicate is checked once immediately before ever sleeping at all -- if the condition is already true by the time wait is called (because the notification that would have signaled it already happened), the thread proceeds immediately without needing to catch a signal that already passed.
questions.professionalAnswer: Two separate problems, one fix. A spurious wakeup means the OS can wake your thread for no real reason at all, and without a predicate you'd proceed as if something actually happened. A missed notification means notify_one() can fire before the consumer even starts waiting, and a bare wait has no way to recover that lost signal. The predicate overload handles both because it's really a loop: check the condition, and only actually sleep if it's false, then re-check after any wakeup, spurious or not. That's why I never call the bare wait(lk) overload in real code -- the predicate version is strictly safer and costs nothing extra to write.

Assuming notify_one() always reaches a thread that is already waiting, ignoring the missed-notification race
Checking the condition once before calling wait but not re-checking it after waking up

A missed notification means notify_one() called before the waiter starts waiting is simply lost
The predicate overload of wait checks the condition in a loop: before sleeping and after every wakeup
This single mechanism correctly handles both spurious wakeups and missed notifications

Correctly explains how the predicate overload fixes both

questions.title: The ABA Problem in a Lock-Free Stack
questions.prompt: Explain the ABA problem in the context of a lock-free singly-linked stack built on compare-and-swap, and why the standard fix (hazard pointers or a version-tagged pointer) is more than a minor implementation detail.
questions.modelAnswer: In a CAS-based lock-free stack, a push or pop reads the current head pointer, computes a new head, and tries to CAS the new value in only if head is still what was read. The ABA problem occurs when a thread reads head as pointer A, gets suspended before its CAS runs, and while it's asleep another thread pops A, frees that node, and a subsequent push happens to allocate a brand-new node at the exact same memory address A (a real possibility with a typical allocator reusing recently-freed memory). When the original thread wakes and runs its CAS, it sees head is still A -- bit-for-bit identical to what it read -- so the CAS succeeds, even though the actual node at that address is now completely different data with a different next pointer. The CAS's only guarantee is 'the bits are unchanged,' not 'nothing happened in between,' and ABA is exactly a case where something happened and the bits came back around anyway. This isn't a minor edge case to patch over -- it can corrupt the stack's structure in a way that's extraordinarily hard to reproduce, since it requires a specific unlucky interleaving plus a specific allocator reuse pattern. The standard fixes address the real problem (distinguishing 'same address' from 'same identity'): tagging each pointer with a monotonically incrementing version counter that's included in the CAS comparison, so a freed-and-reallocated node at the same address still has a different tag; or hazard pointers, which let a thread announce 'I'm currently examining this pointer' so it won't be freed out from under it at all, sidestepping the problem rather than detecting it after the fact.
questions.professionalAnswer: The core issue is that CAS can only tell you 'the value is still what I last saw,' not 'nothing happened since I last looked.' ABA is exactly the case where a thread gets suspended, the node it was holding onto gets freed and reused by a new allocation at the same address, and the thread wakes up and sees the same bit pattern and happily proceeds as if nothing happened -- except the actual object there is now something else entirely. That's a real structural corruption risk, not a cosmetic bug, and it's why I'd never hand-roll a lock-free stack without either a version-tagged pointer or hazard pointers -- or, more realistically, without just using a reviewed library that's already solved this correctly.

Assuming CAS failing to detect ABA is itself a bug in CAS, rather than an inherent limitation of comparing bit patterns
Underestimating how rarely and unpredictably ABA reproduces, which makes it dangerous precisely because it passes most testing
keyPoints: CAS only verifies the compared value's bit pattern is unchanged, not that nothing happened in between
ABA occurs when a pointer is freed and a new allocation reuses the exact same address
The resulting corruption is a real structural bug, not a performance nuance
Fixes: version-tagged pointers (included in the CAS) or hazard pointers (preventing reuse while referenced)

questions.title: Sizing Task Granularity for a Thread Pool
questions.prompt: A thread pool is submitted a thousand tasks, each pricing a single option (a few microseconds of work). Throughput is worse than single-threaded. Explain why, and what change to the task granularity would actually help.
questions.modelAnswer: A thread pool's overhead per submitted task -- acquiring the queue's mutex, pushing the task, notifying a worker, the worker acquiring the mutex again, popping, and releasing -- is itself real, measurable work, typically on the order of hundreds of nanoseconds to low microseconds depending on contention. When each task's actual payload is only a few microseconds, that coordination overhead is a large fraction of, or even larger than, the work itself, so the pool spends more time managing tasks than doing them, and overall throughput is worse than just running everything serially with zero coordination cost. The fix is to increase task granularity: instead of submitting one task per option, chunk the thousand options into, say, the number of worker threads (or a small multiple of it) batches, with each task pricing a whole batch of options in a tight loop. That amortizes the fixed per-task coordination cost across far more actual work per task, which is exactly the trade-off the thread-pool lesson's rule of thumb -- aim for tasks that take at least tens of microseconds -- is getting at.
questions.professionalAnswer: The pool isn't broken, the task size is just too small for the overhead it has to pay every time -- locking the queue, pushing, notifying, a worker waking up and popping, all of that is real time that doesn't scale down to zero just because the actual work is tiny. With a few-microsecond payload, that overhead can dominate, which is exactly why performance gets worse, not better. The fix is to chunk: submit roughly one task per worker thread, each one pricing a batch of a few hundred options in a plain loop, instead of a thousand tiny tasks. That amortizes the fixed coordination cost across way more real work per task, which is the actual lever here, not the thread pool's implementation.
commonMistakes: Blaming the thread pool's implementation instead of the task granularity
Assuming more parallelism is always better regardless of per-task work size
Not recognizing that per-task coordination overhead (locking, queuing, notifying) is itself real, measurable cost

A thread pool can be slower than serial execution if tasks are too fine-grained
The fix is chunking work into larger batches, roughly one task per worker rather than one per unit of work
A reasonable rule of thumb is tens of microseconds of real work per submitted task, at minimum

questions.title: Struct-of-Arrays vs. Array-of-Structs for a Risk Calculation
questions.prompt: A risk engine needs to sum just the notional field across a million Position records, each of which also has a symbol, a delta, and a gamma. It currently uses an array-of-structs layout. Explain the cache-level reason to switch to struct-of-arrays for this specific access pattern, and when array-of-structs would actually be the better choice instead.
questions.modelAnswer: With an array-of-structs layout, each Position record (notional, symbol, delta, gamma all together) occupies one contiguous block, so every cache-line fetch while summing notional across a million records also pulls in symbol, delta, and gamma for that record -- bytes that get fetched into cache and then never used for this particular calculation, wasting a large fraction of the cache line's useful bandwidth. A struct-of-arrays layout instead stores one contiguous array per field (a notional array, a separate symbol array, a separate delta array, a separate gamma array), so summing notional touches only the notional array -- every single byte fetched into cache is a notional value actually needed for the sum, with zero waste. For this specific workload -- scanning one field across many records -- struct-of-arrays wins decisively, often by several times, purely from better cache-line utilization, with no algorithmic change at all. Array-of-structs would be the better choice instead for a different access pattern: if the typical operation is 'look up position 442 and use all of its fields together' (print a full record, compute something that genuinely needs notional, delta, and gamma for the same position at once), array-of-structs keeps everything needed for that single record in one or two cache lines, whereas struct-of-arrays would scatter the same logical record across four separate, unrelated memory locations.
questions.professionalAnswer: The reason array-of-structs loses here is that summing just notional still drags symbol, delta, and gamma along for the ride on every cache-line fetch, because they're all physically interleaved in memory -- that's wasted cache bandwidth on every single record. Struct-of-arrays fixes that by putting each field in its own contiguous array, so scanning notional touches only notional, nothing else. I'd flip the recommendation the moment the access pattern flips too, though -- if the real workload is 'grab everything about position 442 at once,' array-of-structs is actually better, because then you want one record's fields sitting together in one or two cache lines, not scattered across four separate arrays.

Not explaining the specific cache-line-waste mechanism, just asserting 'SoA is faster'
Missing that array-of-structs is the right choice when records are accessed as whole units

Array-of-structs wins when a typical access needs all fields of one record together

questions.title: const, constexpr, and the Optimizer: More Than Style
questions.prompt: Explain how marking a value const can unlock compiler optimizations that wouldn't otherwise be safe, and what constexpr adds beyond that. Use a repeated read inside a hot loop as the example.
questions.modelAnswer: Marking a value const is information the compiler can act on, not just the reader: if the optimizer can prove nothing is able to modify a value between two reads of it inside a loop, it can hoist that read out of the loop entirely and reuse a cached copy, instead of re-reading it on every iteration. Without const, the compiler has to be conservative -- unless it can otherwise prove no aliasing pointer or reference could have modified that value, it may be forced to re-read it every time, just in case something changed it between iterations. const removes that uncertainty for the compiler the same way it documents intent for a human reader. constexpr goes a step further: it asks for the value to be computed entirely at compile time wherever possible, so a function like constexpr double basis_points_to_decimal(double bps) { return bps / 10000.0; } called with a literal argument produces a value baked directly into the binary as a constant -- there's no runtime division at all, not even once, because the entire computation happened while compiling, not while running. const only helps the optimizer reason about mutation; constexpr can eliminate the computation from runtime altogether.
questions.professionalAnswer: const gives the optimizer a guarantee it can actually use: if nothing can change this value, a repeated read inside a loop can be hoisted out and done once instead of every iteration, because the compiler no longer has to assume, conservatively, that something might have mutated it in between. constexpr is a bigger lever -- it's not just 'this won't change,' it's 'compute this entirely at compile time if you can,' so a constexpr function called with a compile-time-known argument produces a literal baked into the binary with zero runtime cost, not even a division. I treat const as the default habit for anything that isn't meant to change, and reach for constexpr specifically when a value is genuinely knowable at compile time.

Confusing const (can't be reassigned) with constexpr (computed at compile time)
Assuming constexpr always guarantees compile-time evaluation even with a runtime-only argument

questions.title: Numba vs. a Hand-Written C++ Extension: Making the Call
questions.prompt: A Monte Carlo simulate_path loop is confirmed, via profiling, to be the actual bottleneck in a Python research pipeline. A teammate wants to jump straight to a pybind11 C++ extension; you suggest trying Numba's @njit first. Make the case for trying Numba first, and say when you'd actually go to C++ instead.
questions.modelAnswer: Numba's @njit compiles an ordinary-looking Python loop to machine code on first call, with no separate build step, no new syntax, and no change to the function's calling convention -- you keep writing explicit, readable loops and let the compiler do the work vectorization would otherwise force by hand. For a function made of arrays, loops, and arithmetic -- exactly what a Monte Carlo path simulation is -- Numba routinely reaches speeds competitive with, and sometimes faster than, a hand-written C++ extension, with a fraction of the engineering cost: no PYBIND11_MODULE boilerplate, no build system, no separate compiled artifact to version and distribute. The case for trying it first is almost pure cost-benefit: if @njit gets you most or all of the speedup needed, you've avoided an entire category of ongoing maintenance (a C++ codebase, a build pipeline, ABI compatibility across Python versions) for free. The case for going straight to C++ instead is when Numba's nopython-mode restrictions are the actual blocker, not its speed -- if the function needs to call into pandas, work with arbitrary Python objects, interact with an existing C/C++ library, or needs features Numba's limited subset of Python simply doesn't support, no amount of tuning Numba will get there, and a pybind11 extension is the right next step. The decision isn't 'Numba is slower, use C++ when speed really matters' -- it's 'try Numba first because its restrictions, not its speed, are usually the actual limiting factor.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd try Numba first purely on cost-benefit grounds: it's a decorator, no build step, no new language, and for a loop made of arrays and arithmetic -- which is exactly what a Monte Carlo path sim is -- it's routinely as fast as, sometimes faster than, hand-written C++, for a fraction of the ongoing maintenance cost. I'd only reach for pybind11 and C++ once Numba's restrictions, not its speed, become the actual blocker -- needing to call pandas, work with arbitrary Python objects, or wrap an existing C/C++ library are the real signals to move, not just 'this still isn't fast enough,' because in my experience that second case is rarer than people assume once they've actually profiled and isolated the real hot loop.

Jumping to a C++ extension before trying the much cheaper Numba option on a confirmed, isolated hot loop
Not recognizing that Numba's real limitation is its restricted language subset, not raw speed

Numba avoids the ongoing maintenance cost of a separate C++ build pipeline and ABI concerns

Profile and isolate the hot loop first, then try the cheaper option before the more expensive one

questions.title: When a Team Actually Needs kdb+ Instead of DuckDB/Parquet
questions.prompt: A trading desk currently uses DuckDB and Parquet for research and is debating whether to invest in kdb+/q for a new project. What's the actual deciding factor, and why is 'the data is time-series' not a sufficient reason on its own?
questions.modelAnswer: DuckDB and Parquet already handle the overwhelming majority of research workloads extremely well -- batch-style analysis over daily or minute-bar data, files that fit comfortably on one machine's disk -- with essentially zero setup cost and excellent measured performance, specifically because they're columnar and match the aggregate-across-many-rows shape most research queries actually have. 'The data is time-series' describes almost everything a research desk touches, so it can't be the deciding factor on its own, or every project would reach for kdb+. The actual deciding factor is the combination of genuinely high-frequency, continuously-arriving data and a latency requirement measured in microseconds to low milliseconds against data that's still being written -- live risk or market-making infrastructure that needs sub-millisecond answers against data streaming in right now, not an end-of-day batch job. kdb+ earns its real cost (a steep learning curve for q, a specialized and largely proprietary ecosystem, licensing) specifically for that ingestion-and-latency profile, not merely because a dataset happens to be large or time-ordered -- DuckDB handles 'large' and 'time-series' just fine on their own, as long as the data isn't also continuously arriving with a hard sub-second latency requirement on top.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd push back on 'it's time-series data' as the justification, because that describes almost everything this desk already handles fine in DuckDB and Parquet. The actual question is about ingestion and latency: is this genuinely high-frequency data arriving continuously, with queries that need sub-millisecond answers against data that's still being written right now? That's the profile kdb+ is actually built for, and it's a real, different problem from 'we have a lot of time-series data and want to analyze it,' which DuckDB already handles well and cheaply. If it's just 'another research dataset,' it isn't.

questions.title: Implement a Single-Producer/Single-Consumer Order Queue
questions.prompt: Implement a thread-safe order queue where a producer thread pushes integer order IDs and a consumer thread processes them as they arrive, using a mutex and a condition variable correctly -- including correct shutdown behavior when the producer is done.
questions.modelAnswer: The queue needs a std::mutex protecting the underlying std::queue<int>, a std::condition_variable the consumer waits on, and a shutdown flag so the consumer knows to stop waiting once the producer is truly finished (otherwise it would wait forever after the last item). The producer locks the mutex with a lock_guard, pushes the order ID, unlocks (scoping the lock_guard tightly), then calls notify_one(); when done, it sets the shutdown flag under the lock and calls notify_one() (or notify_all(), since multiple consumers might be waiting) one more time so a consumer currently waiting wakes up and sees the shutdown condition. The consumer uses a std::unique_lock (required by condition_variable::wait) and calls cv.wait(lk, [&]{ return !queue.empty() || done; }) -- the predicate form, so spurious wakeups and missed notifications are both handled correctly -- then checks whether it woke because there's real work (pop and process it) or because of shutdown with nothing left (exit the loop).
questions.professionalAnswer: The shape is: a mutex-protected queue, a condition variable, and critically a shutdown flag so the consumer doesn't wait forever after the producer finishes. Producer side: lock, push, unlock, notify_one -- and one final notify after setting the done flag so a currently-waiting consumer actually wakes up to see it. Consumer side: unique_lock plus the predicate overload of wait, checking both !queue.empty() and the done flag, then distinguishing 'there's real work' from 'we're done and empty' after waking up. The predicate form is doing double duty here -- it's both the standard spurious-wakeup/missed-notification protection and the mechanism that lets clean shutdown actually work.

questions.title: Implement submit() for a Minimal Thread Pool
questions.prompt: Given a ThreadPool class with a fixed set of worker threads already created in its constructor, implement submit(std::function<void()> task) and the worker loop it feeds, so submitted tasks are picked up and run by whichever worker is free.
questions.modelAnswer: submit() needs to push the task onto a shared, mutex-protected queue and wake a worker: lock the mutex, push the task (moved, not copied, since std::function can wrap an arbitrary, possibly expensive-to-copy callable), unlock, then call notify_one() so exactly one idle worker wakes to handle it. Each worker thread runs a loop that waits (using the predicate form of condition_variable::wait, to correctly handle spurious wakeups and the stop condition) until there's a task available or the pool is stopping; once woken with real work, it pops the task under the lock, unlocks, and runs the task outside the lock so that running the task doesn't block other workers from acquiring the queue. The loop then repeats, waiting again for the next task.
questions.professionalAnswer: submit() is just: lock, push the task, unlock, notify_one. The more interesting part is the worker loop -- each worker waits on the predicate overload for 'there's a task, or we're stopping,' pops under the lock if there's real work, unlocks before actually running the task (so running it doesn't hold up anyone else trying to submit or pop), and loops back to wait again. The one detail that's easy to get wrong is running the task while still holding the lock -- that would serialize every task behind the single queue mutex, defeating the entire point of having multiple workers.

questions.title: Using a Profiler Output to Decide What's Actually Worth Porting
questions.prompt: cProfile on a research pipeline shows 90% of cumulative time inside pandas.DataFrame.groupby, and a separate line_profiler run on a custom simulate_path function shows 95% of its own time on one line doing per-element Python arithmetic. A teammate wants to port the groupby call to C++. What would you actually recommend, and why?
questions.modelAnswer: Porting the groupby call would be the wrong move: pandas's groupby is already backed by compiled C code, so the 90% of cumulative time it shows isn't time spent in slow, interpreted Python bytecode -- it's time spent doing real, already-fast aggregation work. Wrapping a call to an already-C-backed operation in a new C++ extension buys essentially nothing, because the bottleneck was never the Python interpreter loop in the first place; it adds a build dependency and boundary-crossing overhead for no real speedup. The simulate_path finding is the opposite, legitimate case: line_profiler pointing at 95% of time on one specific line of pure-Python, element-by-element arithmetic is exactly the signature of a genuinely interpreter-bound hot path -- this is real wall-clock time spent executing Python bytecode in a loop, which is precisely what a Numba @njit or a pybind11 C++ port is good at eliminating. The recommendation is to leave the groupby call alone entirely and focus porting effort on simulate_path, porting the whole per-path loop (not just the one hot line) so the boundary is crossed once per batch of paths rather than once per element.

questions.title: Write a Point-in-Time ASOF JOIN for Last Known Price
questions.prompt: Using DuckDB, write a SQL query that, for each row in a requests table (a timestamp and a symbol), finds the most recent price at or before that timestamp from a prices table. Explain why a plain JOIN on equal timestamps would be wrong here.
questions.modelAnswer: A plain equality JOIN (ON r.symbol = p.symbol AND r.ts = p.ts) would only match rows whose timestamps are exactly identical, which almost never happens for an arbitrary request time against discrete price ticks -- most requests would simply match nothing. ASOF JOIN solves this directly: for each row on the left (requests), it finds the single best-matching row on the right (prices) at or before the left row's timestamp, using the condition r.req_ts >= p.ts. This is exactly the 'last known value as of this timestamp' pattern, and getting it right matters for a specific correctness reason: a naive join or window-function trick that accidentally matched a price from after the request time would hand the query information that wasn't actually available yet at that moment -- the same look-ahead bias problem as in backtesting, just expressed as a SQL join.
questions.professionalAnswer: A plain equality join only matches rows with the exact same timestamp, and request times almost never land exactly on a tick, so most rows would just come back empty. ASOF JOIN is built specifically for 'give me the most recent row at or before this time,' which is exactly the point-in-time lookup this needs. The reason to get this right rather than hack around it with a correlated subquery is correctness, not just convenience -- matching a price from after the request time would be handing the query information it couldn't have actually had yet, which is the same look-ahead-bias mistake as in a backtest, just showing up as a SQL bug instead.
questions.example:
SELECT r.req_ts, r.symbol, p.ts AS as_of_ts, p.price AS last_known_price
FROM requests r
ASOF JOIN prices p
  ON r.symbol = p.symbol AND r.req_ts >= p.ts;

Accidentally matching a price from after the request time, introducing look-ahead bias

questions.title: Writing a Typed Cython Loop, and Knowing When It's the Right Tool
questions.prompt: Sketch a Cython .pyx function, using cdef-typed variables and a typed memoryview, that computes a rolling variance over a NumPy array faster than pure Python. Then explain a case where Cython is the right choice specifically over Numba, not just a slower-to-set-up alternative.
questions.modelAnswer: Declaring the loop counters and accumulators with cdef (cdef int i, cdef double total) makes them genuine C-level int/double variables at compile time, not Python objects -- removing the per-element Python-object overhead a plain Python loop pays on every single arithmetic operation. A typed memoryview (double[:] returns) gives Cython a C-level view directly onto the NumPy array's underlying buffer, so indexing into it is a fast, direct memory access rather than going through Python-level indexing machinery. Cython needs this all compiled ahead of time via setup.py/cythonize or pyximport, unlike Numba's runtime JIT. The case where Cython is specifically the right choice over Numba, not just a less convenient alternative, is when the hot function needs to do something Numba's nopython mode fundamentally can't: calling into an existing C or C++ library directly, working with arbitrary Python objects (not just NumPy arrays and numeric scalars) inside the loop, or shipping a compiled extension as a distributable package without depending on Numba's JIT machinery being installed and working at runtime on whatever system it ends up running on.
questions.professionalAnswer: The sketch is straightforward: cdef the loop variables and accumulators so they're real C types, use a typed memoryview to get direct, fast access to the NumPy array's buffer, and let cythonize/build_ext compile it ahead of time. Where I'd actually reach for Cython over Numba isn't 'this needs to be a bit faster' -- it's when Numba's nopython-mode restrictions are the actual blocker: wrapping an existing C/C++ library, needing arbitrary Python objects inside the hot loop instead of just arrays and scalars, or shipping a compiled package where I don't want a runtime JIT dependency at all. If none of those apply, I'd try Numba first; it's just less setup for comparable speed on array-and-loop-shaped code.
questions.example:
# rolling_vol.pyx (illustrative)
import numpy as np

cdef double _variance(double[:] chunk, int window):
    cdef double total = 0.0
    cdef int k
    for k in range(window):
        total += chunk[k]
    cdef double mean = total / window
    cdef double sq_total = 0.0
    for k in range(window):
        sq_total += (chunk[k] - mean) ** 2
    return sq_total / window

cpdef rolling_vol_cython(double[:] returns, int window):
    cdef int n = returns.shape[0]
    cdef int i
    out = []
    for i in range(window, n):
        out.append(_variance(returns[i - window:i], window) ** 0.5)
    return out
commonMistakes: Leaving loop variables as plain Python objects instead of cdef-declaring them, losing most of the speed benefit
Treating Cython as simply 'Numba but with a build step' rather than understanding its distinct capabilities
Choosing Cython by default instead of trying Numba first for ordinary array/loop-shaped numeric code

A typed memoryview gives direct, fast access to a NumPy array's buffer
Cython requires an ahead-of-time build step, unlike Numba's runtime JIT
Cython is the right choice specifically when Numba's nopython-mode restrictions, not just its speed, are the blocker

questions.title: Parallelizing a CPU-Bound Backtest Sweep Correctly
questions.prompt: You need to run the same backtest across 200 different parameter combinations, each taking about 2 seconds of pure CPU-bound work. Write the ProcessPoolExecutor code to parallelize this correctly, and explain why threads would not have helped here.
questions.modelAnswer: Threads wouldn't help because CPython's Global Interpreter Lock allows only one thread to execute Python bytecode at a time, regardless of how many CPU cores are available -- for CPU-bound work like a backtest loop, multiple threads just take turns on one core rather than running truly in parallel, so wrapping this in a ThreadPoolExecutor would show no real speedup. ProcessPoolExecutor sidesteps the GIL entirely by running each task in its own separate process, each with its own full Python interpreter and its own GIL, so the OS can genuinely schedule them across multiple cores simultaneously. With 200 tasks at roughly 2 seconds of real CPU-bound work each, the per-task overhead of process creation and argument/result pickling is comfortably small relative to the actual work, which is exactly the task-granularity profile where multiprocessing pays off rather than backfiring. The if __name__ == '__main__': guard is required (and safe everywhere) because spawning a worker process re-imports the module, and without the guard that re-import would try to spawn the pool again, recursively.
questions.professionalAnswer: Threads are out because of the GIL -- for CPU-bound work, Python threads just take turns on one core no matter how many cores you have, so a ThreadPoolExecutor here would show basically no speedup. ProcessPoolExecutor actually works because each worker is its own full process with its own interpreter and its own GIL, so the OS can really run them on separate cores. At roughly 2 seconds of real work per task across 200 tasks, the fixed overhead of spinning up processes and pickling arguments back and forth is small relative to the actual computation, which is exactly the profile where this approach pays off instead of backfiring the way it would on a thousand tiny tasks.

def run_backtest(params):

    ...
    return result

if __name__ == "__main__":

    with ProcessPoolExecutor(max_workers=4) as ex:

questions.title: Diagnosing a Deadlock From Inconsistent Lock Ordering
questions.prompt: Two functions each need to lock both a PositionBook mutex and a RiskLimits mutex. One function locks PositionBook then RiskLimits; another locks RiskLimits then PositionBook. The system occasionally hangs completely under load. Diagnose the bug and the fix.
questions.modelAnswer: This is a classic deadlock from inconsistent lock ordering: if thread A locks PositionBook and is about to lock RiskLimits, while thread B simultaneously locks RiskLimits and is about to lock PositionBook, each thread ends up waiting forever for a lock the other thread is holding, and neither can ever proceed -- a permanent, total hang, not a transient slowdown. It's intermittent under load specifically because this requires a genuinely unlucky interleaving (both threads reaching their second lock attempt at roughly the same time), which is rare enough to pass casual testing but inevitable eventually under real concurrent traffic. The reliable fix is enforcing a single, consistent global lock-acquisition order everywhere in the codebase that needs both locks -- for example, always lock PositionBook before RiskLimits, never the reverse, in every function, so the specific circular-wait pattern that causes deadlock can never arise. A more robust alternative is std::lock(mutexA, mutexB), which acquires multiple locks together using a deadlock-avoidance algorithm, removing the need to manually enforce ordering discipline across the whole codebase by hand.
questions.professionalAnswer: Classic lock-ordering deadlock: one code path locks A then B, another locks B then A, and under the right unlucky timing each one ends up holding one lock while waiting for the other, forever. That's why it's intermittent and load-dependent -- it needs both threads to hit their second lock at close to the same moment, which is rare in light testing but will eventually happen under real traffic. The fix is enforcing one consistent lock order everywhere -- always A before B, no exceptions -- or using std::lock() to acquire both together with its own deadlock-avoidance algorithm instead of relying on everyone remembering the right manual order.

Fixing the ordering in only one of the two functions instead of enforcing it everywhere both locks are needed

questions.title: Diagnosing False Sharing in a Multi-Threaded Counter Array
questions.prompt: A per-thread array of eight std::atomic<long> counters, one per worker thread, shows terrible scaling -- adding more threads makes it slower, not faster, even though each thread only ever touches its own counter. What's going on?
questions.modelAnswer: This is false sharing: even though each thread only logically touches its own counter, if the eight counters are packed tightly together in one array, several of them physically share the same 64-byte CPU cache line. Every write to any one counter invalidates that entire cache line in every other core's cache, forcing those cores to re-fetch the line from a slower cache level or memory the next time they access their own counter -- even though no actual data race or logical conflict exists between the threads. The result looks exactly like lock contention (worse scaling as more threads pile on) despite there being no lock and no shared logical data at all; it's purely a side effect of the physical memory layout. The fix is padding each counter out to its own cache line, typically 64 bytes, so no two counters from different threads ever land in the same cache line -- for example wrapping each counter in a small struct with explicit padding bytes, or using alignas(64) on each counter, or simply spacing the array elements far enough apart that false sharing becomes structurally impossible.
questions.professionalAnswer: That symptom -- more threads, worse performance, with zero actual data race -- is the signature of false sharing. The counters are logically independent, but if they're packed into one tight array, several of them physically sit in the same CPU cache line, and a write to any one of them invalidates that whole line for every other core, forcing an expensive re-fetch even though nothing about the actual data conflicted. It looks exactly like lock contention from the outside, but there's no lock anywhere. The fix is padding each counter out to its own cache line -- alignas(64) per counter, or a padded struct -- so no two threads' counters can ever collide in the same cache line again.

Fixing it by adding locking, which addresses the wrong problem and adds real overhead for no benefit

questions.title: Diagnosing Thread Pool Starvation From Oversized Tasks
questions.prompt: A thread pool with 4 workers is submitted a mix of many small pricing tasks and a few large, several-second batch-revaluation tasks. Small tasks that should finish almost instantly sometimes take seconds to even start. What's happening, and how would you fix it?
questions.modelAnswer: A basic thread pool with a single FIFO task queue has no concept of task priority or size -- if a large, several-second task happens to be dequeued by one of the four workers, that worker is simply unavailable for the next several seconds, regardless of how many tiny, fast tasks are waiting behind it in the queue. With only 4 workers, if 1 or 2 of them get tied up on long tasks, the remaining small tasks either queue up behind other small tasks on the remaining workers or, worse, a small task that happens to be scheduled onto a worker just after a long task starts has to wait for that long task to finish before even being picked up. This is a form of head-of-line blocking / starvation, not a bug in the pool's correctness -- it's doing exactly what a simple FIFO pool is designed to do, which just doesn't match a workload with very different task sizes. The fix is typically one of: a separate, dedicated pool (or a reserved subset of workers) for small, latency-sensitive tasks so they're never queued behind long-running ones; breaking large batch-revaluation tasks into smaller chunks that interleave more fairly with small tasks; or a priority queue instead of plain FIFO, so small, latency-sensitive tasks can jump ahead of already-queued long tasks when that's the actual requirement.
questions.professionalAnswer: This isn't a bug, it's exactly what a plain FIFO thread pool does when task sizes vary wildly -- a long-running task ties up one of your four workers for its full duration, and anything queued behind it on that worker just has to wait, no matter how fast it would otherwise finish. With only 4 workers, losing even one or two to multi-second tasks noticeably starves the small ones. I'd fix this with either a separate pool for latency-sensitive small tasks so they're never stuck behind a long one, or by chunking the big batch-revaluation work into smaller pieces that interleave more fairly, or a priority queue if small tasks genuinely need to jump the line.

questions.title: Debugging 'Parallelized' Python Code With No Actual Speedup
questions.prompt: A teammate parallelized a CPU-bound feature-engineering loop using Python's threading module and ThreadPoolExecutor, expecting a 4x speedup on a 4-core machine, but measured almost no improvement at all. Diagnose the cause.
questions.modelAnswer: The root cause is CPython's Global Interpreter Lock: only one thread can execute Python bytecode at a time, regardless of core count, so for genuinely CPU-bound work -- a tight computation loop, not something waiting on I/O -- multiple Python threads don't run truly in parallel, they take turns on a single core. Threads are legitimately useful in Python specifically for I/O-bound work, where waiting on a network request or disk read releases the GIL while waiting, letting other threads run meanwhile -- but a feature-engineering loop doing real computation the whole time never releases the GIL in a way that benefits from more threads. The fix is switching to multiple processes instead of threads: concurrent.futures.ProcessPoolExecutor runs each worker in its own separate process, each with its own full Python interpreter and its own independent GIL, so the OS can genuinely schedule them across multiple cores at once. The one thing to verify first is that the per-task work is large enough to be worth the real overhead of process creation and pickling arguments/results -- multiprocessing has its own granularity requirement, just a different one than threading's GIL problem.

The fix is ProcessPoolExecutor instead of a thread pool -- separate processes, separate interpreters, separate GILs, which actually lets the OS use multiple cores.
