questions.title: Investigating Unexpectedly High Execution Shortfall
questions.prompt: A VWAP execution algorithm is consistently costing 15+ basis points versus arrival price, far worse than the near-zero shortfall seen in backtesting. Walk through how you'd investigate whether the algorithm itself, or something else, is the actual cause.
questions.modelAnswer: The first thing to check is whether the backtest's near-zero shortfall was itself realistic or an artifact: a VWAP simulation that sizes its slices using the day's realized volume (which is only known after the fact) will match its own benchmark almost perfectly, but a real VWAP algo has to size slices against a predicted volume profile built from historical averages, and only matches the realized benchmark as well as that prediction turns out to be -- a mismatch here isn't a live bug at all, it's an unrealistic backtest. Assuming the backtest's volume-prediction methodology was sound, the next step is decomposing the 15+ bps into its actual sources: how much is genuine market drift during the execution window (which both TWAP and VWAP are equally exposed to and isn't the algorithm's fault), versus how much is the algo's own slices consistently executing worse than the volume-weighted benchmark it was targeting. If the predicted volume curve used for slicing is systematically wrong for this instrument (e.g. built from a different instrument's typical U-shaped profile, or stale), the algo would be mis-timing its slices relative to when liquidity is actually available, which directly produces exactly this kind of persistent shortfall. The investigation should compare live fills against both the arrival-price benchmark and the algo's own intraday VWAP benchmark separately, since conflating the two obscures whether the problem is market drift or genuinely bad execution timing.
questions.professionalAnswer: First question: was the backtest's near-zero number even realistic? If it sized VWAP slices using the day's own realized volume, that's cheating relative to what a live algo can actually know in advance -- it's only working from a predicted volume curve, so a real shortfall gap against that kind of backtest isn't necessarily a live bug. Assuming the backtest methodology was fair, I'd split the 15+ bps into market drift (which hits any algo equally and isn't the algorithm's fault) versus the algo's own fills consistently missing its own VWAP benchmark -- and if it's the latter, I'd check whether the predicted volume curve it's slicing against actually matches this instrument's real intraday liquidity pattern, because a stale or wrong volume profile would explain exactly this kind of persistent, structural shortfall.

questions.title: Investigating a Realized-vs-Expected Volatility Alert
questions.prompt: A live strategy's realized daily P&L volatility is running at 1.8x its backtested expectation, but the kill switch hasn't triggered because no single day has breached the hard loss limit. How do you investigate this, and should it have triggered something regardless?
questions.modelAnswer: A realized/expected volatility ratio of 1.8x is squarely a 'review, not kill switch' signal: kill switches exist for hard, pre-committed single-day or cumulative-drawdown limits, while a volatility ratio this elevated is exactly the kind of softer anomaly that's supposed to generate an alert to a human rather than an automatic stop, specifically because it doesn't automatically mean the strategy is broken -- a single unusually volatile period (one bad day, a short-lived regime shift, a data glitch inflating one day's P&L swing) can move a short-sample ratio substantially without the strategy actually having changed in any fundamental way. The investigation should first rule out sampling noise: how many days is this ratio computed over, and would removing the single worst day change the picture significantly -- if so, this may be exactly the kind of short-sample volatility the monitoring lesson warns against over-reacting to. If the elevated ratio persists over a longer, sustained window rather than being driven by one outlier day, that's a real signal worth treating seriously -- it could indicate the strategy's actual risk profile live doesn't match what the backtest predicted, which is often an early sign of the kind of decay that eventually warrants a retirement review. Separately, yes, something should have triggered regardless of whether the hard kill-switch limits were breached -- this is exactly the gap between hard limits and softer alerts that the monitoring discipline is supposed to cover, and if no alert fired at 1.8x, that threshold itself may need to be set as an explicit, pre-committed alert trigger rather than only relying on someone noticing it.

questions.title: Debugging a Spurious -50% Day in a Backtest
questions.prompt: A backtest shows a strategy taking a sudden, massive one-day loss on a date that corresponds to a known 2-for-1 stock split, even though the strategy never actually held a losing position that day. Diagnose the cause.
questions.modelAnswer: This is the classic unadjusted-price bug: a 2-for-1 split halves the raw, unadjusted close price overnight with zero actual change in the company's value, and a backtest computing returns from raw close.pct_change() instead of the split-adjusted adj_close sees that halving as a genuine 50% one-day loss -- pure data artifact, not anything the strategy actually did. The fix is using adjusted close prices for return calculations, which retroactively rescale historical prices so splits (and, for total-return analysis, dividends) don't appear as fake price jumps. One subtlety worth checking at the same time: if the strategy's signal logic trades on absolute price levels (a rule like 'buy if price > $50'), the adjusted series isn't necessarily the right one for that trigger logic, since an adjusted price series itself changes retroactively as new dividends are paid -- the correct pattern is generally unadjusted prices for level-based trade triggers and adjusted prices specifically for computing realized P&L and returns.

The fix is switching return calculations to the adjusted close, which has already been rescaled backward through history to remove exactly this kind of artifact. One thing I'd double check at the same time: if any part of the signal trades on absolute price levels rather than just returns, I'd want unadjusted prices for that trigger logic specifically, since the adjusted series itself shifts over time as new dividends get paid.

questions.title: Diagnosing a Stale-Answer Bug From an Incomplete Cache Key
questions.prompt: A disk-cached expensive_backtest(signal_name, lookback, cost_bps) function was recently changed to add a new cost_bps parameter, but the cache key was never updated to include it. What breaks, and why might it not be noticed immediately?
questions.modelAnswer: If the cache key is still only (signal_name, lookback) after cost_bps was added as a real input that affects the result, two calls with the same signal_name and lookback but genuinely different cost_bps values will collide on the exact same cache entry -- the second call, instead of recomputing with its own cost_bps, silently returns the first call's cached result, computed under a different cost assumption entirely. This is a stale wrong answer, not a cache miss, which is specifically the worse of the two cache-key failure modes: a too-narrow key (missing an input that matters) returns incorrect data confidently, with no error, no warning, and no symptom that looks like a bug from the outside. It might not be noticed immediately because the first call that populates the cache for a given (signal_name, lookback) pair establishes whatever cost_bps happened to be used that first time, and every subsequent call with a different cost_bps silently inherits that stale result -- the bug only becomes visible if someone happens to notice that changing cost_bps doesn't actually change the reported result, which is easy to miss unless specifically tested for. The fix is updating the cache key to include every argument that actually affects the output: (signal_name, lookback, cost_bps).
questions.professionalAnswer: This is the dangerous cache-key failure mode: too narrow a key, not too wide. Since cost_bps was added as a real input but never added to the key, two calls that differ only in cost_bps collide on the same cache entry, and the second one silently gets the first one's answer under a completely different cost assumption -- no error, no warning, just a confidently wrong number. It can go unnoticed for a while because nothing about calling it looks broken; you'd only catch it by specifically testing that changing cost_bps actually changes the result, which is easy to skip if you're not looking for it. The fix is just adding cost_bps to the cache key so it's included in every lookup and every stored entry.

questions.title: Designing Reproducible Logging for a Research Pipeline
questions.prompt: A research pipeline's Sharpe ratio report from six months ago can no longer be reproduced, and nobody remembers the exact config, seed, or library versions used. Design the minimum logging discipline that would have prevented this.
questions.modelAnswer: The minimum discipline is: every run of a pipeline that produces a result anyone might later need to reproduce should, at the moment it starts, log the exact resolved configuration actually used (not just 'loaded config from file,' but the real parameter values), the random seed, and the versions of the key libraries involved (at minimum numpy/pandas and anything with its own randomness or numerically-significant behavior) -- all through Python's logging module at INFO level, not print(), so the record is structured, timestamped, and filterable rather than scattered. This should happen automatically, as part of the pipeline's normal execution, not as a manual step someone has to remember to do separately, because the entire point is that it needs to exist even for the run nobody thought was important at the time. Architecturally, this pairs with a lockfile (pinning exact dependency versions for a given environment) and, ideally, a config file checked into version control for non-secret settings, so that six months later, 'what produced this number' has an actual, written answer: the logged seed and config from that specific run, combined with the lockfile or logged versions, gives everything needed to reconstruct the exact environment and inputs.
questions.professionalAnswer: The fix has to be automatic, not a habit someone's supposed to remember: every run logs its actual resolved config values, its seed, and the key library versions, right at the start, through logging rather than print so it's structured and timestamped. That has to happen on every run, including the ones that don't feel important yet, because by definition you don't know in advance which result someone's going to ask about again in six months. questions.title: Why a src/ Layout Prevents a Specific Import Bug
questions.prompt: A research package works fine when run from the repo root but breaks with a confusing import error once a teammate installs it properly and runs it from a different directory. Explain the specific bug class a src/ layout prevents, and why a flat layout is vulnerable to it.
questions.modelAnswer: With a flat layout (the package directory sitting directly at the repo root, next to pyproject.toml), running Python from the repo root adds the current directory to Python's import path, which means import quant_research can silently succeed by importing the uninstalled local package directly off the filesystem, even if the package was never actually pip-installed at all, or was installed incorrectly. This masks real packaging problems: the code appears to work perfectly for the person who happens to always run it from exactly that directory, while the exact same import fails or behaves differently for anyone running it from somewhere else, or after a proper install, because there the current-directory trick isn't available and the import has to go through whatever was actually, correctly (or incorrectly) installed. A src/ layout (the package living under src/quant_research/ rather than at the root) eliminates this shortcut entirely: there's no way for the current-directory import trick to find the package, so every import -- in development, in testing, for every teammate, from every directory -- is forced to go through the real, installed package, via pip install -e . in editable mode for active development. The bug class this prevents is exactly 'it works on my machine because I happen to be in this one directory' quietly papering over a packaging problem that then surfaces, confusingly, for someone else.
questions.professionalAnswer: The flat layout has a specific trap: running from the repo root adds that directory to Python's import path, so import quant_research can succeed by grabbing the local, uninstalled package straight off disk -- even if the real pip install never actually worked correctly. That looks fine for whoever always happens to run it from that exact directory, and then breaks confusingly for anyone else, or after a real install, because the shortcut isn't available anywhere else. Moving the package under src/ removes that shortcut entirely -- there's no path by which Python finds it except through the actual, installed package, so pip install -e . either genuinely works for everyone or fails loudly right away, instead of working by accident for one person.

questions.title: Designing a Test Suite for a Numerical Returns Function
questions.prompt: Design a test suite (not just one test) for a pct_returns(prices) function, covering both the correctness-assertion pitfall and the edge cases numerical code commonly mishandles.
questions.modelAnswer: The suite needs several distinct categories of test, not just one happy-path case. First, a basic correctness test using pytest.approx or np.testing.assert_allclose rather than == -- comparing computed floats with == fails on values that are mathematically correct but not bit-identical due to floating-point rounding, which is a bug in the test, not the code, and would otherwise produce a confusing false failure. Second, explicit edge-case tests: an empty array and a single-element array (both should return zero results, not crash or return something nonsensical), an input containing NaN (which should propagate through to the corresponding output positions, not silently vanish or produce a different NaN-adjacent wrong value), and, if realistic for the domain, very large magnitude values that could risk overflow. Third, ideally a property-based test using hypothesis that checks a general rule across many generated inputs -- for example, that the output length is always exactly one less than a non-empty input's length -- which catches combinations of input size and magnitude that hand-picked test cases never happen to try. Designing the suite this way, as distinct categories rather than one or two example-driven tests, is what actually catches the kinds of bugs that pass casual, happy-path-only testing.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd think of it as several distinct categories, not just 'a few tests.' Tolerance-based assertions (pytest.approx / assert_allclose) instead of == for the basic correctness check, since == on floats fails for the wrong reason -- rounding, not a real bug. Explicit tests for empty input, a single-element input, and NaN propagation, since those are exactly the inputs numerical code quietly mishandles. And ideally a hypothesis property test checking something that should always hold -- like output length always being input length minus one -- across a lot of generated inputs, which catches combinations nobody thought to hand-write. The real value here is in the categories, not any single test.

Not considering a property-based test to cover combinations hand-picked examples wouldn't catch

questions.title: Should This Sharpe-Ratio Script Be a Class?
questions.prompt: A teammate wraps a one-off script that loads a CSV, computes a Sharpe ratio, and prints it into a SharpeCalculator class with an __init__ and a calculate() method. Is that a good use of OOP here? Contrast it with a PositionBook that tracks fills over time.
questions.modelAnswer: A class earns its place when there's state that persists and changes over time, with behavior tied to that state -- a PositionBook is exactly this: holdings change as fills arrive, and 'what's my current exposure' is a question that needs the current, evolving state, not a fresh recomputation from nothing each time, so bundling that state with the methods that update and query it (add_fill, total_value) is genuinely useful. The SharpeCalculator case has none of that: load a CSV, compute one number, print it -- there's no persisting state across calls and no behavior beyond the single calculation itself. Wrapping it in a class with __init__ and calculate() adds ceremony (an object to construct, state to manage even though nothing's actually changing) without adding anything a plain function wouldn't already do, more simply. The right question isn't 'could this be a class' -- almost anything technically could be -- it's 'does this genuinely have state and behavior that benefit from being bundled together, or is this just adding structure the problem doesn't need.' Here, a plain function does the same job with less code to read and maintain.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd push back on the class here. The test I use is: is there real state that persists and changes, with behavior attached to it? A PositionBook clearly has that -- positions change as fills come in, and querying current exposure needs that live state. A script that loads a CSV, computes one Sharpe ratio, and prints it has none of that; there's nothing persisting, nothing changing, just one calculation. Wrapping it in a class adds an object to construct and 'state' that never actually changes, for no real benefit over a plain function. The question isn't whether it could be a class -- almost anything could -- it's whether the structure is actually earning its complexity here, and in this case it isn't.

questions.title: Choosing Columnar Storage for a Research Data Layer
questions.prompt: A research team's data layer currently stores tick data in a traditional row-oriented database designed for an application's transactional workload. Queries like 'average price by symbol across 2 million rows' are slow. Diagnose why, and justify switching to a columnar approach like Parquet/DuckDB.
questions.modelAnswer: A row-oriented database stores all columns of one row together on disk, which is the right layout for a transactional (OLTP) access pattern -- 'fetch this one specific order, with all its fields' -- but it's the wrong layout for an analytical (OLAP) query like 'average the price column across 2 million rows,' because that query has to read every column of every row off disk even though it only actually needs one or two of them, wasting most of the I/O on data it never uses. A columnar store like Parquet inverts this: all values of one column are stored together, so an aggregate query over just price and volume reads only those columns' bytes, skipping symbol and anything else entirely. This also compounds with two further benefits: compression works much better on a column of similar values than on a row interleaving different types, and a vectorized query engine like DuckDB can run SIMD-friendly operations across a contiguous chunk of one column at once. The research team's query pattern -- aggregate, analytical, across many rows -- is almost always OLAP-shaped, essentially never 'fetch and update one specific record,' which is exactly the mismatch explaining the current slowness and exactly the case columnar storage is built for.
questions.professionalAnswer: The slowness is a storage-layout mismatch, not a sizing problem. Row-oriented storage is built for 'fetch one record with all its fields,' which is a transactional pattern -- but an 'average price by symbol' query is analytical, and in a row store that means reading every column of every row off disk just to use one or two of them. Parquet/DuckDB's columnar layout flips that: the query only reads the columns it actually needs, plus you get real compression and vectorized execution benefits on top. Research queries are almost always this analytical, aggregate-across-many-rows shape, which is exactly the mismatch explaining the current slowness and exactly what columnar storage is designed to fix.

Treating compression and vectorized execution as separate, unrelated benefits rather than both following from the columnar layout

Columnar storage reads only the needed columns, matching the analytical/aggregate access pattern

Research queries are almost always OLAP-shaped (aggregate across many rows), rarely OLTP-shaped

questions.title: Designing a Correct Cache Key for a Research Pipeline Step
questions.prompt: Design the caching layer for an expensive_backtest(signal_name, lookback, cost_bps, data_version) pipeline step, including what the cache key must contain and how you'd guard against the single biggest risk in doing this wrong.
questions.modelAnswer: The cache key must include every single argument that actually determines the output -- here, (signal_name, lookback, cost_bps, data_version) -- no more and no less. Including an irrelevant input makes the key too specific, causing avoidable cache misses for calls that should actually hit; the far more dangerous mistake, though, is omitting an input that genuinely affects the result, since that makes two different, legitimately different calls collide on the same stored entry, and the second call silently receives the first call's answer computed under different conditions -- a confidently wrong result with no error or warning, which is specifically why 'cache invalidation' has its own reputation as a genuinely hard problem, not a trivial implementation detail. data_version deserves particular attention here: if the underlying historical data is ever revised or extended, a cache key that doesn't account for which data version produced a given result would serve a stale answer computed against now-outdated data, indefinitely, with no way to tell from the outside. A disk-based cache (via diskcache) is the right persistence layer so results survive across process restarts and scheduled runs, not just within one session. The concrete guard against the biggest risk is a simple discipline: every time a new parameter is added to the underlying function that could change its output, it must be added to the cache key in the same change, reviewed as part of that same code change rather than as an afterthought.
questions.professionalAnswer: The key has to be exactly (signal_name, lookback, cost_bps, data_version) -- every real input, nothing more. The dangerous failure mode isn't too many cache misses, it's a key that's missing one of these: two genuinely different calls collide on one stored entry, and the second one silently gets the first one's answer under different conditions, with zero error or warning. data_version is the one I'd watch most carefully here, since if the underlying data ever gets revised, a cache that doesn't account for that would happily serve a stale result computed against outdated data forever. The actual discipline that prevents this: any time a new parameter gets added to the function, adding it to the cache key is part of that same change, not a follow-up task someone might forget.

questions.title: Where the Execution-Algorithm Layer Belongs in the System
questions.prompt: A strategy currently generates a target position and calls OrderManager.submit() directly for the full size in one order. The desk wants to start using VWAP execution for larger orders. Where architecturally should that TWAP/VWAP logic live, and why shouldn't the strategy's own code implement the slicing?
questions.modelAnswer: The slicing logic belongs inside the execution/OMS layer, as a distinct execution algorithm the strategy can request, not inside the strategy's own code. The strategy's actual job is deciding what to trade and how much -- producing a target position -- and that decision is conceptually independent of how the resulting order gets worked into the market. If every strategy that needs VWAP slicing implemented its own slicing loop, the same non-trivial logic (volume-curve prediction, implementation-shortfall tracking, slice timing) would be duplicated and could easily drift out of sync across strategies, and a single bug or improvement in that logic would need to be found and fixed in every strategy separately rather than once. The correct interface is something like OrderManager.submit(target, algo=VWAP) or a dedicated execution-algorithm layer the OMS calls into, so the strategy just states what it wants (a target position, optionally with an execution style) and the execution layer handles the actual mechanics of getting there -- exactly the same separation-of-concerns argument that justifies the OMS abstraction existing at all between strategies and broker protocols.
questions.professionalAnswer: This belongs in the execution/OMS layer, not in the strategy. The strategy's job is deciding what to trade and how much; how that gets worked into the market -- all at once, TWAP, VWAP -- is a separate, genuinely reusable concern that shouldn't be duplicated inside every strategy that happens to need it. If each strategy implemented its own VWAP slicing, a bug or improvement in that logic has to be found and fixed everywhere it was copied, instead of once. The clean interface is something like submit(target, algo=VWAP) on the OMS side, so the strategy just states its intent and the execution layer owns the actual mechanics -- the same reasoning that justifies having an OMS abstraction at all.

questions.title: Architecting an Automated Strategy Retirement Review Process
questions.prompt: Design a system component that automatically flags a live strategy for retirement review based on rolling Sharpe decay, rather than relying on someone remembering to check periodically. What are the key design decisions, and why does the threshold need multiple consecutive checks rather than one?
questions.modelAnswer: The component needs, at minimum: a recomputed rolling-window Sharpe ratio (refreshed on a regular cadence, e.g. monthly), a pre-committed numeric threshold below which performance is considered concerning, and critically, a requirement that the rolling Sharpe stay below that threshold for several consecutive checks, not just one, before flagging a review. The multiple-consecutive-checks requirement exists specifically to avoid reacting to short-term noise: a single bad monthly window can push a rolling Sharpe below any reasonable threshold even for a strategy that's perfectly healthy, just from ordinary sampling variation, and a system that flags a review on the very first below-threshold reading would generate frequent false alarms that erode trust in the alerting system itself. Requiring, say, three consecutive monthly checks below the threshold means a short-lived rough patch self-corrects before triggering anything, while a genuine, sustained decline still gets caught within a reasonable window -- a deliberate tradeoff between reacting fast (and risking false alarms) and reacting slow (and giving up more capital to a genuinely decayed strategy) that should be set deliberately, the same way kill-switch thresholds are, rather than picked arbitrarily. Just as important: flagging a review should never mean automatically shutting the strategy down -- it should route to a human decision (pause and re-paper-test, resize, or retire), since the system's job is surfacing the signal reliably, not making the final call.
questions.professionalAnswer: The key pieces are a rolling-window Sharpe recomputed on a regular cadence, a pre-committed threshold, and -- this is the part people skip -- requiring several consecutive below-threshold checks, not just one, before flagging anything. A single bad month can push even a healthy strategy's rolling Sharpe below a reasonable threshold purely from noise, and reacting to that single reading would generate false alarms that eventually make people stop trusting the system. Requiring three consecutive checks lets a short rough patch self-correct while still catching a genuine, sustained decline in a reasonable window -- that's a deliberate speed-vs-false-alarm tradeoff, set on purpose, the same way kill-switch thresholds are. And I'd make sure flagging a review routes to a human decision, not an automatic shutdown -- the system's job is surfacing the signal reliably, not making the retirement call itself.

questions.title: Leading a Blameless Postmortem After a Production Incident
questions.prompt: A bug you reviewed and approved caused a strategy to double-submit orders for twenty minutes before anyone noticed. You're asked to lead the postmortem. How do you run it?
questions.modelAnswer: A good postmortem is structured around what happened and why the systems and process allowed it, not around assigning individual blame -- even though you personally reviewed and approved the change, starting from 'whose fault is this' produces defensiveness and incomplete information, while starting from 'what sequence of events, checks, and gaps let this happen' produces an honest, complete timeline people are willing to contribute to. Concretely: build an exact timeline (when the bug was introduced, when it was reviewed, when it shipped, when double-submission started, when it was detected, when it was fixed), identify every point a different check could plausibly have caught it (code review, a specific missing test case, a monitoring alert that didn't exist or didn't fire, a kill switch that could have caught the resulting anomaly but wasn't tuned to), and come away with concrete, assigned action items -- not vague 'be more careful' resolutions, but specific changes: add this test, add this monitoring check, adjust this threshold. As the reviewer who approved the change, explicitly owning that part of the timeline without being defensive about it actually sets the tone for everyone else to be equally honest about their own part, which is what makes the whole process actually work.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd run it blameless by design -- not ignoring that I reviewed and approved the change, but framing the whole thing around 'what sequence of events and gaps let this happen,' not 'whose fault is it.' Concretely: a precise timeline from when the bug was introduced through when it was caught, a specific look at every point something could have caught it earlier -- review, a missing test, monitoring that didn't fire -- and ending with concrete, owned action items, not 'be more careful.' I'd also make a point of openly owning my part of the timeline first, without being defensive about it, because that's what actually gives everyone else permission to be honest about their part instead of covering for themselves.

questions.title: Negotiating a Quant Developer Offer With a Researched Range
questions.prompt: You've received an offer from a prop trading firm with a lower base and a profit-share component you don't fully understand yet, and a competing offer from a bank desk with a higher, steadier base. Walk through how you'd actually negotiate and decide, rather than just comparing the two base numbers.
questions.modelAnswer: Comparing base numbers alone is comparing the wrong thing here, since prop shops and bank desks structure total compensation very differently -- a prop shop's lower base with a profit-share component tied to individual or desk PnL can pay far more in a good year and far less in a bad one than a bank desk's steadier, less individually-PnL-linked bonus on a higher base, so the real comparison needs to be expected total compensation and its variance, not the headline base. Before negotiating anything, I'd build a researched range for each firm type and city from a couple of independent sources -- aggregated salary sites read skeptically, actual live postings for comparable roles, and candid input from my own network, since quant pay is unusually city- and firm-type-sensitive and general sources underrepresent it. With that range in hand, a respectful counter follows the same shape that works anywhere: thank them for the offer, state the researched range with a specific, concrete reason behind it (not just 'I want more'), and stay collaborative rather than issuing an ultimatum. The actual decision between the two offers, once the numbers are properly understood, should weigh my own tolerance for the prop shop's compensation variance against the bank desk's steadier structure, alongside non-compensation factors -- which firm's research/risk culture and mentorship actually fit what I want, and what the role concretely does day to day, since the same title can mean very different things at each firm.
questions.professionalAnswer: The base numbers alone aren't actually comparable here -- a prop shop's profit-share-heavy structure and a bank desk's steadier bonus are different risk profiles wrapped around different compensation shapes, so I'd be comparing expected total comp and its variance, not just the headline base. Before I negotiate anything, I'd build a researched range per firm type and city from a couple of independent sources, since general salary sites underrepresent quant-specific roles. Then a respectful counter: thank them, state the range with a specific reason, stay collaborative. And the actual decision isn't just math -- it's how much variance I can personally tolerate, plus which firm's culture and mentorship I actually want, since the same job title can mean something very different at each place.

questions.title: Mentoring a Junior Developer Through a Recurring Memory Bug
questions.prompt: A junior developer on your team keeps introducing dangling-pointer bugs, and their latest fix for one was to add a try/catch around the crash rather than addressing the actual lifetime issue. How do you mentor them through this effectively?
questions.modelAnswer: The try/catch 'fix' is a strong signal the junior developer doesn't yet have a working mental model of object lifetime, not just that they made one careless mistake -- catching an exception around undefined behavior doesn't actually address it (dangling-pointer dereferences aren't even guaranteed to throw a catchable exception in the first place), so pointing that out concretely, with why it doesn't fix the real problem, is the necessary first step rather than skipping straight to the lifetime explanation. From there, the more effective long-term move is walking through one or two of their actual recent bugs together, asking them to trace exactly when each object was created and destroyed rather than lecturing abstractly about stack vs. heap -- people build real intuition for lifetime from tracing concrete examples, not from hearing the rule restated. It's also worth normalizing that this is a genuinely common category of mistake for anyone newer to C++, not a sign they're not cut out for it, while still being clear that the pattern (not just this one bug) needs to change, and following up on their next few PRs specifically for this issue rather than assuming one conversation fixed it.
questions.professionalAnswer: The try/catch is the real tell here -- it means they don't have a working model of lifetime yet, not just that they made one mistake. I'd point out directly, concretely, why that doesn't actually fix anything -- dangling-pointer UB isn't even guaranteed to throw something catchable. Then I'd walk through one or two of their actual recent bugs together and have them trace exactly when each object gets created and destroyed, rather than re-explaining stack vs. heap in the abstract -- that's where the real intuition comes from. I'd also tell them directly this is a common mistake at this stage, not a sign they're bad at this, while being clear the pattern itself needs to change, and I'd actually follow up on their next couple of PRs rather than assuming one talk fixed it.
commonMistakes: Only pointing out that the try/catch doesn't fix the bug without addressing the underlying lifetime misunderstanding
Re-explaining the abstract rule (stack vs. heap) instead of tracing concrete examples from their actual code
Assuming one conversation resolves a recurring pattern, without following up on subsequent work
keyPoints: A try/catch around undefined behavior doesn't fix it and signals a deeper lifetime misunderstanding
Tracing concrete examples from the developer's own recent bugs builds real intuition better than abstract explanation
Normalize that this is a common mistake at this experience level, while being clear the pattern must change
Follow up on subsequent work rather than assuming one conversation resolved a recurring pattern

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the try/catch as addressing the wrong problem, and explains why
Proposes tracing concrete examples rather than abstract re-explanation
Balances supportive tone with clear expectation the pattern must change
Mentions following up on subsequent work

questions.title: Pushing Back on an Unrealistic Backtest Engine Rewrite Deadline
questions.prompt: Leadership wants the team's backtest engine rewritten from vectorized to event-driven architecture, with full feature parity, in two weeks, to unblock a new strategy that needs path-dependent logic. You believe this realistically takes six weeks. How do you handle this?
questions.modelAnswer: The right move is to separate the actual business need (unblocking the new strategy) from the specific solution leadership proposed (a full rewrite with full feature parity), because those aren't the same thing, and the gap between them is exactly where a faster, legitimate path might exist. A two-week full rewrite with complete feature parity across a mature vectorized engine is a genuinely different, much larger scope than 'make it possible to backtest this one path-dependent strategy soon' -- the latter might be achievable in two weeks via a narrower, targeted approach (a small, purpose-built event-driven harness for just this strategy, without replacing the existing vectorized engine's other users) while the full rewrite proceeds on a realistic six-week timeline in parallel. Presenting this as a concrete tradeoff -- here's what a two-week narrow solution gets you, here's what the full six-week rewrite gets you, here's the risk of trying to force full parity into two weeks (corners cut on testing, a rushed engine other strategies then depend on) -- gives leadership an actual decision to make with the real costs visible, rather than either quietly agreeing to an unrealistic deadline and cutting corners, or just flatly saying no without offering a path to the thing they actually need.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd separate what they actually need from what they asked for -- unblocking one path-dependent strategy is not the same scope as a full-parity rewrite of the whole engine, and that gap is where a faster real option probably lives. I'd propose a narrow, purpose-built event-driven path just for this one strategy, deliverable in something closer to the two-week window, while the full rewrite proceeds on its real six-week timeline in parallel. Then I'd lay out the actual tradeoff plainly: here's what the narrow fix gets you now, here's what full parity costs and why rushing it risks shipping something other strategies end up depending on without enough testing. That gives leadership a real decision instead of me either quietly agreeing to something I don't believe, or just saying no.
commonMistakes: Treating the stated solution (full rewrite) as fixed, instead of questioning whether it's actually required to meet the real need
Simply agreeing to the unrealistic deadline and cutting corners on testing
Flatly refusing without offering any concrete path toward what leadership actually needs sooner
keyPoints: Separate the actual business need from the specific solution proposed, since they may not require the same scope
Propose a narrower, faster solution if one genuinely addresses the real need
Present the tradeoff (narrow fast fix vs. full proper rewrite) explicitly, with real costs and risks named
Avoid both silently agreeing to an unrealistic deadline and simply refusing without an alternative

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly separates the underlying need from the proposed solution's scope
Proposes a concrete, narrower alternative to meet the real deadline
Presents the tradeoff explicitly rather than silently complying or flatly refusing
Professional tone

questions.title: Disclosing a Bug You Introduced Into Production
questions.prompt: You discover, two days after deploying your own change, that it introduced a subtle sizing bug that's been slightly overstating position sizes in a live strategy since the deploy. No one else has noticed yet. What do you do?
questions.modelAnswer: The only acceptable move is disclosing it immediately and fully, to whoever owns risk/oversight for that strategy, the moment it's discovered -- not waiting to investigate quietly first and only surfacing it once there's a complete picture, since the strategy continues running with the sizing error for every additional hour that passes undisclosed, and that ongoing exposure is the actual risk, not the embarrassment of reporting an incomplete picture. The disclosure should be factual and specific: what the bug is, when it was introduced, the estimated magnitude and duration of the sizing error so far, and an immediate recommendation (pause the strategy, or at minimum flag it for urgent review) while the full fix and impact assessment continue in parallel. It's worth being honest that this was your own change without over-apologizing or getting defensive -- the goal in the moment is accurate, fast information that lets the right people make a risk decision, not managing how the mistake reflects on you personally; that part gets addressed properly afterward, in the postmortem.
questions.professionalAnswer: I disclose it immediately, fully, to whoever owns risk for that strategy -- not after I've quietly dug in and have a complete picture, because every extra hour it's live and undisclosed is the actual risk, not how complete my report is. I'd be factual: what broke, when, roughly how much and for how long, and an immediate recommendation like pausing it while the full fix and impact assessment continue. I'd own that it was my change without being defensive or over-apologizing in the moment -- what matters right then is getting accurate information to the people who need to make a risk call, not managing how it looks for me. That gets sorted out properly in the postmortem afterward.
commonMistakes: Waiting to investigate quietly before disclosing, extending the strategy's ongoing undisclosed exposure
Disclosing vaguely instead of giving a specific, factual account of the bug's magnitude and duration
Getting defensive or over-apologizing instead of focusing on giving the information needed for a risk decision
keyPoints: Disclose immediately upon discovery, not after quietly investigating to a complete picture
Every additional hour undisclosed is real ongoing risk, which outweighs the discomfort of an incomplete report
Disclosure should be factual and specific: what, when, estimated magnitude/duration, and an immediate recommendation
Own the mistake without being defensive, focusing on actionable information over managing personal reputation in the moment

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly recommends immediate disclosure rather than quiet investigation first
Describes a factual, specific disclosure with an immediate recommendation
Shows accountability without defensiveness
Clarity

questions.title: Working With a Researcher Who Dismisses Testing as Overhead
questions.prompt: A quant researcher you support keeps pushing untested, hand-verified-only signal code straight into the shared research library, saying unit tests 'slow down research.' Their code has already caused two silent bugs that reached production backtests. How do you address this?
questions.modelAnswer: The productive approach is making the cost concrete rather than arguing abstractly that 'testing is good practice' -- pointing specifically at the two actual incidents this exact pattern already caused, including what each one cost (time spent diagnosing, any decisions made on a wrong number before it was caught), is far more persuasive than a general principle, because it directly counters the 'tests slow down research' framing with 'and untested code has already cost us this much, twice.' It's also worth proposing something lighter than what the researcher is probably imagining when they hear 'unit tests' -- a small number of well-chosen edge-case tests (empty input, a known reference value) on just the parts of their code that get reused by others, not a demand for full test coverage on every piece of exploratory analysis, since exploratory, one-off research code genuinely has a different risk profile than shared library code other people depend on. Framing it as 'code that other people build on deserves a slightly higher bar than your own scratch notebook' is a distinction most researchers find reasonable once it's made explicit, rather than experiencing it as a blanket process demand. If this doesn't resolve through direct conversation, escalating with the concrete incident history (not vague frustration) to whoever owns the shared library's standards is the legitimate next step.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't argue the abstract case for testing -- I'd point at the two actual incidents this exact pattern already caused, with what each one cost, because that directly answers 'tests slow down research' with 'and this has already cost us real time, twice.' I'd also propose something much lighter than full coverage -- a handful of well-chosen tests, just on the parts of their code that other people actually build on, not their exploratory one-off analysis, which genuinely doesn't need the same bar. Most researchers find that distinction reasonable once it's made explicit, rather than hearing it as a blanket process demand. If it still doesn't land, I'd escalate with the actual incident history, not just general frustration, to whoever owns the shared library's standards.
commonMistakes: Arguing the abstract principle ('testing is good practice') instead of pointing at concrete, already-happened incidents and their cost
Demanding full test coverage on all of the researcher's code, including genuinely exploratory analysis that doesn't need it
Escalating with vague frustration instead of specific incident history
keyPoints: Ground the argument in the concrete cost of the two actual incidents, not an abstract principle
Propose a lighter, targeted testing bar specifically for shared library code, not all exploratory research
Distinguish shared, reused code's risk profile from one-off exploratory analysis explicitly
Escalate with concrete incident history, not vague frustration, if direct conversation doesn't resolve it

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Grounds the argument in the concrete cost of the actual past incidents
Proposes a reasonable, targeted testing scope rather than full coverage everywhere
Distinguishes shared code from exploratory research appropriately
Describes a reasonable escalation path if needed

questions.title: Deciding Whether to Escalate a Code-Quality Concern
questions.prompt: During a routine refactor, you notice that a core risk-limit check has a logic error that makes it slightly less conservative than intended -- it's not causing visible problems today, but it's technically wrong. Fixing it properly would take a day you don't currently have budgeted, and nobody's asked you to look at this code. What do you do?
questions.modelAnswer: A logic error in a risk-limit check is squarely in the category of things that must be surfaced immediately, regardless of whether it's currently visible or in scope for the task at hand -- risk-limit code exists specifically to catch the scenario where something else has already gone wrong, so a bug there is a bug in the safety net itself, and 'it hasn't caused a visible problem yet' is exactly the property a latent risk-control bug has right up until the day it matters. The right move is not to silently fix it (if it takes longer than available time, a quick unreviewed fix to critical risk code is its own risk) and not to silently ignore it because it's out of scope -- it's to report it immediately to whoever owns that code or the team's risk process, with a concrete, specific description of exactly how it's less conservative than intended, and let them decide the priority and timeline for the proper fix, rather than making that call unilaterally just because it's inconvenient today. This is exactly the kind of finding that's worth surfacing even though 'nobody asked you to look at this' -- the value of noticing it doesn't depend on whose task it technically was.
questions.professionalAnswer: This gets reported immediately, full stop -- a bug in a risk-limit check is a bug in the actual safety net, and 'no visible problem yet' is precisely the state a latent risk-control bug sits in right up until it matters. I wouldn't quietly patch it myself under time pressure either, since a rushed, unreviewed fix to critical risk code is its own risk, and I wouldn't let 'nobody asked me to look at this' be a reason to just move on. I'd flag it specifically -- exactly how it's less conservative than intended -- to whoever owns that code or the risk process, and let them make the call on priority and timeline, rather than deciding unilaterally that it can wait because fixing it properly isn't convenient today.
commonMistakes: Deciding unilaterally that it can wait because it hasn't caused a visible problem yet
Attempting a quick, unreviewed fix to critical risk-limit code under time pressure instead of reporting it
Ignoring the finding because it was outside the scope of the assigned task
keyPoints: A bug in a risk-limit check is a bug in the safety net itself and must be surfaced immediately
'No visible problem yet' is exactly the state a latent risk-control bug has until it matters
A rushed, unreviewed fix to critical risk code under time pressure is its own risk
Report the finding specifically and let the code's owner decide priority, rather than deciding unilaterally

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly treats this as requiring immediate escalation, not a 'can wait' judgment call
Correctly avoids a rushed, unreviewed self-fix under time pressure
Describes a specific, concrete report rather than a vague mention
Clarity
